t: Management Profiles: Berkeley Nucleonics Leadership
d: Meet the Berkeley Nucleonics management team, the second-generation leaders behind the company's precision test and measurement instruments since 1963.
words: About Us · Leadership Management Profiles The people who lead Berkeley Nucleonics, and the founders whose work still shapes how we build. Current Management A second-generation team with deep roots in the products we make. David Brown President David Brown has led Berkeley Nucleonics as president since 2001, seven years after joining, and has spent that time turning a respected pulse-generator house into one of the broadest signal-source companies in the industry. He drove R&D on the Model 935 SAM isotope identifier, the SAM Defender LaBr radionuclide identifier, and the PB-5 NIM pulse generator, and helped build training programs for the U.S. Air Force. He holds a B.A. in entrepreneurial management from San Francisco State University. Off the clock, David is a devoted basketball fan and a snowboarder, and he has recently taken up gardening with his wife, a project he cheerfully admits is harder than it looks. John Reynolds Vice President of Operations John Reynolds joined Berkeley Nucleonics in 2006 and has been a driving force behind its growth ever since. He runs purchasing, account management, and logistics, and has made the operation measurably faster and leaner as the product range expanded. He holds a B.S. in business marketing from Sonoma State University. Off the clock, John lives in Sonoma County with his wife and three kids, has a deep appreciation for food of every kind, loves rallying the company through competitive team sports, and keeps a personal tie to horse racing. John Lauder Chief Technical Officer John Lauder joined in 2009 as an applications engineer and advanced to chief technical officer, solving the hard problems along the way and launching the company into new areas including RF and microwave. He anchors our most demanding customer relationships and sets the technical direction for the test and measurement lines. Off the clock, John is a traveler drawn to the most obscure corners of the map, and he is never one to back down from a challenge, whether it is a remote destination or a hard problem at the bench. Mark Slattery Nuclear Applications Manager Mark Slattery joined Berkeley Nucleonics in 2008 and leads the nuclear applications team, where he takes on some of the country’s toughest radiation detection and identification problems. t: The Berkeley Nucleonics Story: Precision Since 1963
d: Berkeley Nucleonics has built precision test and measurement instruments since 1963, growing from custom pulse generators into a broad signal-source line.
words: About Us · Our History The Berkeley Nucleonics Story Sixty years of precision instrumentation, from a single custom pulse generator to one of the most diverse signal-source companies in the industry. A company built on precision Berkeley Nucleonics builds precision electronic instrumentation for the people who cannot afford to guess. Test and measurement, radiation detection, nuclear research, RF and microwave: the catalog runs from signal generators and spectrum analyzers to pulse generators, arbitrary waveform generators, and isotope identifiers, one of the widest ranges of signal generation and analysis tools you can get from a single manufacturer. The company is headquartered in San Rafael, California, with additional U.S. facilities and a representative network that reaches more than 60 countries. Our application engineers pick up the phone, and if you want to put a unit on your own bench before you commit, we will set up a demo. A look inside Berkeley Nucleonics Founded in 1963 It started with custom pulse generators. Berkeley Nucleonics built them to tighter tolerances than the market expected, and a reputation for precision, stability, and plain reliability followed. The Model 625A, our first ARB and function generator, was named Test and Measurement Product of the Year by the Cahners Electronics Group. That obsession with waveform fidelity never left. It still shows up in today’s arbitrary waveform generators, which lead the field in modulation bandwidth and memory depth. Innovative engineering Few companies have shaped digital delay generation the way we have. Berkeley Nucleonics has introduced fifteen distinct digital delay generators, with timing resolution down to 250 femtoseconds, and independent media surveys keep ranking us in the top tier of DDG producers year after year. The same engineering runs through our light pulse generators and RF signal generators, all built to one rule: get smaller and faster without giving up performance. The Nuclear Products Group In the mid-1990s we stood up the Nuclear Products Group to take on radiation detection and analysis. In 1997 it delivered the SAM 935, the first real-time system that could identify and quantify several radionuclides at once. Those instruments now work in environmental monitoring, health physics, emergency response, and power generation. We back the hardware with training. Berkeley Nucleonics runs an accredited program of seminars in radiation detection and measurement, in person across the country and online, and by 2020 our teams had trained personnel at more than 165 private, state, and federal sites.

Covers drone-plate installation, sensor-plate assembly, and the safety steps to follow before flight. Medusa MSB-303 · Universal Mounting Plate · Assembly Instructions Contents 1. Overview 2. Compatibility 3. Parts & Components 4. Drone-Plate Installation 5. Sensor-Plate & Detector Mounting 6. Safety Precautions 7. Legacy Plates Replaced 8. Technical Resources 1 Overview The MSB-303 mounts any MS-Series drone-borne detector to a carrier drone or platform. The MSB-303 Universal Mounting Plate is Medusa's current mounting system for the MS-Series drone-borne gamma spectrometers. It is a modular, two-part quick-release plate: a drone-side plate (Part A) that mounts to the carrier, and a sensor-side plate (Part B) sized to the specific detector, joined by a twist-lock carbon-fiber-tube interface. One MSB-303 kit, with the correct Part B for the detector in use, replaces the model-specific plates Medusa previously offered per detector (see Section 7 ). Features One mounting system across the MS-350, MS-700, and MS-1000 Quick-release, twist-and-press coupling for fast attach/detach Rubber-damped carbon-fiber-tube interface for vibration resistance Reference-fit to the DJI Matrice 350 and Matrice 400, adaptable to other carrier platforms This page is Berkeley Nucleonics' summary of Medusa's official MSB-303 assembly instructions, adapted to our documentation format. For the complete, most current procedure and reference drawings, always follow Medusa's official assembly instructions . 2 Compatibility The MSB-303 is compatible with the following Medusa MS-Series detectors carried by Berkeley Nucleonics: Detector Datasheet MS-350 MS Series overview → MS-700 MS Series overview → MS-1000 MS Series overview → Reference drone platforms are the DJI Matrice 350 and DJI Matrice 400 . Per Medusa, the system is not limited to these two — any drone or carrier platform capable of supporting the payload and offering a suitable mounting interface can be used, with possible additional integration work. 3 Parts & Components The MSB-303 kit has two main assemblies: Part A — Drone plate: aluminum plate with integrated carbon-fiber rods; mounts to the drone or carrier. Part B — Sensor plate: aluminum plate sized to the detector; mounts directly to the MS-Series unit. Component Weight Part A — drone plate 126 g Part B — sensor plate, for MS-350 168 g Part B — sensor plate, for MS-700 176 g Part B — sensor plate, for MS-1000 202 g Materials: aluminum plates, carbon-fiber tubes, rubber vibration dampers, stainless-steel fasteners (M3 and M4). Fasteners referenced: M3×25, M3×16, M3×8, and M4×20 screws, plus M3 standoffs/spacers and M4 lock nuts, depending on drone platform and detector. Reference drawings (PDF/DXF) are available from Medusa on request. 4 Drone-Plate Installation General Attach Part A to the drone using existing mounting holes, or a custom adapter if needed. Confirm the mounting surface is rigid and flat before proceeding. Insert the carbon-fiber tubes into the rubber dampers with a twisting motion until seated. Check that both tubes protrude equally on each side. DJI Matrice 400 Place the drone upside down on a protected surface, with sensors shielded from contact. Install the M3×16 spacers into the designated mounting holes. Position the drone plate on the spacers. Insert the M3×25 screws and tighten in a cross (star) pattern for even clamping. Insert the carbon-fiber tubes with a twisting motion, keeping extension symmetric on both sides. Placement for the standoffs. Drone plate positioned and screwed in. Drone plate completely mounted. DJI Matrice 350 Place the drone upside down on a soft, protected surface. Install the M3×10 standoffs into the mounting holes. Position the drone plate on the standoffs. Insert and tighten the M3×8 screws in a cross (star) pattern. If needed, pre-form a pilot hole in the rubber mounts before inserting fasteners. Insert the carbon-fiber tubes with a twisting motion, keeping extension symmetric on both sides. Standoffs installed in the mounting holes. Drone plate attached to the drone. Drone plate completely mounted. Other carrier platforms: follow the General steps above and Medusa's official drawings for hole spacing and fastener sizing specific to that platform. 5 Sensor-Plate & Detector Mounting Sensor-plate assembly (Part B) Insert an M4 lock nut into each corner piece, nut facing downward. Place an M4 washer on top of each nut. Insert the corner pieces into the detector's end caps. Position the sensor plate on the detector. Secure with M4×20 screws, tightening evenly across all corners. Corner-piece orientation: lock nut down, washer on top. Corner pieces in place. Sensor plate completely mounted. Mounting the detector to the drone plate Loosen all thumb screws (counter-clockwise). Align the sensor assembly with the carbon-fiber tubes on the drone plate. Press until the coupling clicks into place. Tighten all thumb screws (clockwise). Verify all four mounting points are secured before proceeding to pre-flight checks. See Medusa's official assembly instructions for a short video of the mount/dismount procedure. 6 Safety Precautions Apply thread-locking compound (medium-strength) to all fasteners to prevent loosening from vibration. Keep the drone powered off for the entire installation. Apply installation force to the mounting system itself, never to the drone frame. Disable any downward-facing sensor on the detector before takeoff. Pre-flight checks Verify the mechanical integrity of the full mounting assembly. Inspect rubber dampers and fasteners for wear before each flight. Confirm downward-facing sensors are disabled via the remote controller. Perform a short test flight before a full survey mission. Disabling the downward-facing sensor from the remote controller's camera view. This section summarizes Medusa's published cautions. Follow Medusa's official assembly instructions for the complete and current safety procedure before every installation and flight. 7 Legacy Plates Replaced The MSB-303 replaces the following model-specific plates, which Medusa has discontinued: MS-350 mounting plate (generic) MS-350 mounting plate (generic quick-release) MS-350 mounting (quick-release, DJI M300/M350) MS-700 mounting plate MS-700 mounting plate (quick-release) MS-700 mounting (quick-release, DJI M400) MS-1000 mounting plate MS-1000 mounting plate (quick-release) 8 Technical Resources MS-Series Data Sheet Test, Measurement and Nuclear Instrumentation since 1963... t: Model 750 Multi-Channel Pulse & Delay Generator
d: The Model 750 packs 4 or 8 independent delay channels, 100 ps (1 ps optional) resolution, and Ethernet/USB remote control into an ultra-compact pulse and delay generator.
words: Model 750 Multi-Channel Pulse & Delay Generator | BNC Skip to main content Product Data Sheet Model 750 Multi-Channel Pulse & Delay Generator An ultra-compact pulse and delay generator with 4 or 8 independent delay channels, 100 ps resolution (1 ps optional), and remote control over USB or Ethernet from any standard browser. 4 or 8 channels 100 ps resolution (1 ps option) USB/Ethernet control 1 Overview The Model 750 provides 4 (or 8, with the channel-extension option) independent delayed pulses. Delays up to 100 seconds can be programmed with 100 ps resolution, with channel-to-channel jitter under 50 ps RMS. An option enhances delay resolution to 1 ps and reduces jitter to under 10 ps RMS. Each output delivers 1.5 V to 5 V pulses with 1 ns rise/fall time into 50 . Pulse amplitude, polarity, width, and burst count are independently adjustable on every channel. Two external trigger inputs or three internal synchronized timers (0.01 Hz to 50 MHz) or a software command can trigger any selected channel, in either single-shot or repetitive mode. A Gate input quickly inhibits selected channel outputs, and can also be configured as a second external trigger or as a link for daisy-chaining two Model 750 units together for additional channels. The Model 750 uses an internal 100 MHz TCXO clock reference, or an external user-programmable clock from 10 MHz to 240 MHz. Front-panel LED indicators show input/output activity, and a RUN/STOP button enables or disables all channel outputs at once. A multi-channel Real-Time Chart View lets you visualize every channel output on a common time chart from a PC, with zoom and cursor tools for precise timing measurement. 2 Key Features 4 independent delay channels (8 with the channel-extension option) 100 ps delay resolution (1 ps with the resolution option) 50 ps channel-to-channel RMS jitter 1.5 V to 5 V output into 50 , 1 ns rise/fall, independently adjustable width, polarity, amplitude, burst, and MUX mode per channel Up to 50 MHz independent trigger rate (single-shot or repetitive) per channel External trigger mode with prescaler, or internal trigger from three synchronous programmable timers, or software command Gate input, selectable as a second trigger or as a daisy-chain link between two units External clocking up to 240 MHz, user programmable USB and Ethernet control, with a browser-based control panel no software install required Ultra-compact, low-power packaging 3 Applications System laser timing control ATE applications Laser pulse picking Precision pulse applications Instrument triggering Component test A common application synchronizes every device in a picosecond laser system from one compact unit and one interface: the Model 750's clock reference input receives a signal from the laser oscillator (via an optical-to-electrical converter). Each amplifier in the chain pump laser, Q-switch, Pockels cell or diagnostic instrument digitizer, calorimeter, camera then receives repetitive or single pulses, independently adjusted in rate, delay, amplitude, polarity, and width, synchronized to that reference with very low jitter. Four GPIO lines under software control add security or low-frequency device interlocks to the same setup. 4 Front & Rear Panel Front panel: 1 5 trigger and channel outputs, 6 power/RUN-STOP switch. Rear panel: 7 gate/trigger, 8 9 clock in/out, A USB/UART, B LAN, C GPIO, D DC power. A trigger controller provides two modes. In external trigger mode, a rising edge on the front-panel TRIG input triggers all delay channels, with each channel's rate set to single-shot, repetitive, or inhibited; a prescaler divides the trigger input frequency by an integer from 1 to 1,000,000,000. In internal trigger mode, delay channels are triggered from three frequency-programmable timers, with each channel's rate again set to single-shot, repetitive, or inhibited. The Gate input quickly inhibits all selected channel outputs, and can alternately be configured as a second external trigger or as an input/output for daisy-chaining two Model 750 units to increase the total channel count. Outputs are designed to drive a 50 load; on a high-impedance load, output level doubles. A burst mode adjusts the number of pulses per trigger via burst count and burst period. A narrow-pulse mode (available with the resolution option) uses a pair of delay channels one to start the output pulse, one to stop it for precisely adjustable pulse widths down to 500 ps. The unit can run stand-alone, without a PC: an Auto-Run option starts output pulses automatically at power-up, and all parameter values are stored in non-volatile memory across 8 selectable user sets. 9 Example of Channel Outputs Mode Mode Repetitive and Single Channel T1 (Repetitive from Timer n 1) Channel T2 (Repetitive from Timer n 2) Channel T3 (Repetitive from Timer n 3) Single shot command Channel T4 (Single pulse from Timer n 3) Mode Burst and Mux Channel T1 (Repetitive from Timer n 1) Channel T2 (Repetitive from Timer n 1, Burst count=3) Channel T3 (Repetitive from Timer n 1 and delay) Delay Channel T4 (Mux = T2+T3) Pulse Picking (synchronized on Timer N 3) External clock (80 MHz for example) Channel T1 (Repetitive from Timer n 1) Channel T3 (Repetitive from Timer n 3) Single shot command Channel T4 (Single pulse picking) 10 Control & Software Two ways to control the Model 750: an easy remote path over Ethernet through an embedded web server, with no software install required, and a general remote path over Ethernet or USB using the included control software or your own application. Easy Remote (Web Control Panel) Via Ethernet and the control panel's web pages, with no specific software application required. The page, served by the unit's embedded web server, provides an easy way to configure every setting. A main menu displays and controls the trigger and clock system (level, slope, prescaler, clock input/output, trigger generators), per-channel delay/width/amplitude/polarity settings, extended settings (burst mode, gate, MUX mode), a RUN button enabling output on all channels, and a Trigger button for a single trigger synchronized to the selected source A parameters menu changes the IP address and other unit-level settings A GPIO menu configures the four input/output lines A Chart View opens a window showing every channel's output on a common time chart in real time, with zoom and cursor tools for detailed timing inspection The instrument stores its own configuration, so the control panel simply reflects it. The page opens in any standard browser (Chrome, Firefox, or Edge): connect the Model 750's Ethernet port to your network, enter the unit's IP address (see the User's Manual) into your browser, and the control panel loads automatically. General Remote (Ethernet/USB) Via Ethernet or USB and a software application (see examples in the User's Manual). A USB application with a GUI similar to the web control panel is included, alongside an ASCII command set over USB (virtual COM port) or Ethernet (TCP port 4000) covering clock configuration, trigger and gate setup, per-channel delay/amplitude/width/polarity/burst/MUX, GPIO, status queries, user-set save/recall, and network configuration. Free Windows and Linux drivers are included. CLOSE

t: Model 750 User Manual
d: Operating guide for the Model 750 mini pulse and delay generator: setup, front/rear panel, remote control over USB and Ethernet, the full ASCII command reference, and hardware options.
words: Model 750 User Manual | BNC Skip to main content User Manual Model 750 User Manual Operating guide for the Model 750 mini pulse and delay generator. Covers setup, front and rear panel, remote control over USB and Ethernet, the full ASCII command reference, and hardware options. Document: User Manual Model 750 Rev. web edition Photo pending rebrand Model 750 product photo to be shot after rebadging. 1 Introduction The Model 750 is a mini pulse and delay generator providing up to 8 independent delayed pulses at up to 50 MHz. The base unit ships with 4 channels; an 8-channel version is available with the channel-extension option. Delays up to 100 seconds can be programmed with 100 ps resolution and channel-to-channel jitter under 50 ps RMS. An option enhances delay resolution to 1 ps. SMB outputs deliver 1.5 V to 5 V, 1 ns rise-time pulses into 50 , with amplitude, polarity, burst count, and width independently adjustable per channel. Two trigger inputs and three internal synchronized timers (0.01 Hz to 50 MHz), plus a software command, can trigger all selected delay channels, each set to single-shot or repetitive. With its multi-trigger system, the Model 750 can be thought of as up to four independent generators in a single box. Power Source and Operating Temperature The supplied power supply operates from 80 V to 264 V AC (47 63 Hz) and delivers +5 V DC at up to 4 A. It is internally earthed to avoid hazardous potential on the case; do not substitute a power supply from another product, and do not apply voltage to the shield or outputs. The Model 750 operates at an ambient temperature of 10 C to 35 C (50 95 F), and can be stored from 10 C to +60 C (15 140 F). It is cooled by air circulation. Power On & Self-Test After connecting power, all front-panel LEDs should be off. A brief press of the front-panel ON/OFF button (which doubles as RUN/STOP) lights the TRIG, channel, and Lock LEDs briefly; the TRIG and channel LEDs then blink for a few seconds before turning off, and the ON/OFF button lights yellow (STOP state). The unit is ready once the Lock LED glows green, indicating the internal system clock is locked. To power off, press and hold the ON/OFF button for more than 5 seconds; all LEDs turn off. If you need further assistance, contact Berkeley Nucleonics technical support at 800-234-7858 or info@berkeleynucleonics.com , and have your unit's serial number ready. 2 Operating Principles Diagram pending rebrand Block diagram: external clock/trigger inputs, time base, trigger controller, 4 (or 8) delay channels, channel outputs, GPIO, USB/Ethernet interface controller, clock output. A time-base function provides a 200 MHz time base from an internal reference or from an external 10 240 MHz reference; the internal time base is also available on the rear-panel clock output. The trigger controller supports two modes: External trigger mode: a rising edge on the front-panel TRIG input triggers all delay channels. Each channel's rate can be single-shot, repetitive, or inhibited. A prescaler divides the trigger input frequency by an integer from 1 to 1,000,000,000. Internal trigger mode: delay channels are triggered from three frequency-programmable timers. Each channel's rate can be single-shot, repetitive, burst, or inhibited. The Gate input quickly inhibits all or selected channel outputs, and can be reconfigured as a second external trigger. The RUN/STOP button enables or disables the output for all delay channels. Delay Channels & Output There are 4 independent delay channels (8 with the channel-extension option). Delay from the selected trigger source is programmable up to 100 seconds, in 100 ps increments (1 ps with the resolution option). Each output pulse (T1 T4, and T5 T8 with the extension option) is independently adjustable in level (1.5 V to 5 V in 10 mV steps), width (10 ns to 10 s in 5 ns steps), and polarity, and may be ORed with other outputs in its group of four. Outputs are designed to drive a 50 load; on a high-impedance load, output level doubles (3.0 V to 10 V). A narrow-pulse mode, available with the resolution option, couples two delay channels one starting the pulse, one stopping it for pulse widths as narrow as 3 ns, precisely and independently adjustable in 1 ps steps. Example Channel-Output Modes The Model 750's trigger sources combine to produce several common patterns: Repetitive and single: different channels independently repetitive from different timers, or single-shot from a software command. Burst and MUX: a channel repeats a burst of N pulses per trigger; a MUX channel ORs two or more channels onto one output. Prescaler and gate: a channel divides down a fast external trigger with its prescaler, while a gate signal inhibits selected channels during part of the cycle. Pulse picking: a single output pulse is picked out of a fast external clock or trigger train, synchronized to one of the internal timers. Delay Jitter & Accuracy Jitter is the delay uncertainty of a channel output edge between successive triggers, measured in RMS picoseconds over an observation period of up to 10 seconds: under 50 ps + delay 10 -7 channel-to-channel, and under 1 ns from an external trigger to any channel. Delay accuracy is the difference between the programmed and measured delay value, referenced against a channel programmed with delay = 0, averaged over 1000 measurements at a 1 kHz rate: under 500 ps + delay 10 -6 . Because per-bank power consumption is limited, some combinations of trigger rate, polarity, and width are restricted between the two channels of a bank (T1/T2, T3/T4, etc). On the 4-channel unit, if one channel in a bank runs above 1 MHz the other must stay at or below 1 MHz (at most 2 channels total may run above 1 MHz); on the 8-channel unit, at most 4 channels total may run above 1 MHz. Within a bank, if one channel's polarity is negative the other must be positive, and if one channel's width exceeds 10 ms the other's must stay under 10 ms. There is no rate limitation when every channel's amplitude is at or below 2.5 V (TTL level). The embedded software checks these automatically before RUN and reports a configuration error if a setting would violate them. Maximum allowed power consumption, internal temperature, and minimum supply voltage are continuously monitored by the embedded software and reported in the control panel's status area. If any value reaches its limit, the overload indicator lights and the unit automatically stops; reduce the trigger rate below 1 MHz to clear the condition, then click the control panel's overload indicator to acknowledge it. The front panel carries a TRIG input, one SMB output per channel, and status LEDs: TRIG (blinks on external trigger), per-channel output LEDs (blink at channel recurrence), RUN/STOP (also the power switch yellow when stopped, green when running), Comm (USB traffic), Ext Clk (running on external clock), and Lock (internal clock system locked, lights green once the unit is ready). Input levels run 1 2.3 V, input impedance is 20 k ; output levels run 0.1 3 V with 100 output impedance and 5 ns rise/fall time. An optional cable breaks the GPIO connector out to a standard DB9. Easy Remote: the Web Control Panel Screenshot pending rebrand Browser control panel: Trigger and Clock System, Delay Channel table, Extended Setup (burst/gate/MUX), Status and Utilities, RUN button, Chart View. After connecting the Model 750's Ethernet port to your network and powering it on, enter the unit's IP address into any standard browser (Chrome, Firefox, or Edge) to open the control panel automatically. The default IP address is 192.168.0.10 , netmask 255.0.0.0 , gateway 192.168.0.1 ; if the address is ever lost, hold the internal reset button (accessible through the rear-panel "RAZ" hole) during power-up to restore it, or query it over USB with NETWORK:IPADDRESS? . The main menu displays and controls the trigger and clock system (level, prescaler, external clock, clock output, three internal generators), the delay channel table (trigger source, rate, delay, amplitude, width, polarity), a RUN button, and a Trigger button for single-shot channels. An Extended Setup panel exposes per-channel burst count/period, gate enable, and MUX grouping. A Parameters page lets you change the IP address and other network settings, and a GPIO page configures the four I/O lines. All settings are stored and saved on the unit itself, so the control panel simply reflects the instrument's current state. The following factory-default values apply out of the box, or after a reset: Parameter Default IP address 192.168.0.10 Gateway 192.168.0.1 Netmask 255.0.0.0 External clock Off (internal reference) External clock frequency 100,000,000 Hz Clock output Off Generators F1 / F2 / F3 10,000 Hz / 1,000 Hz / 1 Hz External trigger 1 / 2 threshold 1500 mV each Rear Gate/Trig input mode Gate Channel trigger source Off Channel trigger rate Single Channel delay / width / amplitude 0 ps / 100 ns / 1500 mV Channel polarity Positive Burst count / period 1 / 200 ns Gate / MUX Off for both Setting Up a First Pulse As a worked example, here is how to produce a repetitive 1 Hz, 5 V, 1 s pulse on channel T1 from the web control panel: Connect the Model 750's Ethernet port to your network and power it on; set your PC's IP address to 192.168.0.100 with netmask 255.0.0.0 , then browse to 192.168.0.10:8080 . Set internal generator F1 to 1.000 Hz. Set channel T1: trigger source F1, rate repetitive, delay 0 ps, width 1000 ns, amplitude 5000 mV, positive polarity. Click RUN . The T1 indicator on the front panel blinks at 1 Hz; confirm the pulse on an oscilloscope, then click STOP to end it. General Remote: USB and Ethernet Over USB, the Model 750 presents a virtual serial (COM) port: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity, no flow control. Any terminal emulator (PuTTY, for example) or the included control application can issue commands directly. Over Ethernet, the same ASCII command set is available on TCP port 4000; set the unit's IP address, netmask, and gateway either from the web control panel's Parameters page or with the NETWORK:* commands described in the Programming Reference below. Free control software is provided for Windows and Linux, presenting the same interface as the web control panel. Both connect over USB and auto-detect the assigned COM port; if the Model 750 is plugged in over USB but not powered on with the front-panel button, the software will see the port but report a connection error until the unit is switched on. 4 Programming Reference Every command below is sent as plain ASCII text terminated with cr lf , over either the USB virtual COM port or an Ethernet connection to TCP port 4000. Delay resolution The smallest step by which a channel's delay can be adjusted 100 ps standard, 1 ps with the resolution option. Gate An input that inhibits selected channel outputs while active; can alternately serve as a second trigger. GPIO General-purpose input/output lines, individually configurable and controlled over the remote command interface, independent of the delay-channel logic. Narrow-pulse mode A mode, available with the resolution option, that couples two delay channels one starting, one stopping the pulse to produce output pulses as narrow as 3 ns.
